caption: Double white lines, solid on your side
colour: two white lines along the road centre, the line nearer you solid, the other broken
explanation: When the white line nearest you is solid (unbroken) you must not cross or straddle it to overtake; you may only cross to pass a stationary obstruction, turn into a side road or premises, or if directed by police.
mnemonic: Solid on your side: stay on your side.
notes: Composite road marking (TSRGD diagram 1013.1 family) drawn in-app; no single official SVG. Solid line on the rider's side prohibits crossing except for the limited exceptions in the Highway Code (rules 128-129).

caption: Hazard warning line
colour: a long white centre line with short gaps (dashes longer than the gaps)
explanation: A centre line with longer dashes and shorter gaps warns of a hazard ahead, such as a bend or junction; do not cross it unless you can see the road is clear and it is safe.
mnemonic: Long lines, short gaps: hazard perhaps.
notes: Composite road marking (TSRGD diagram 1004 family) drawn in-app; no single official SVG. Distinguished from an ordinary centre line by dashes that are longer than the gaps between them (Highway Code rule 127).

caption: Give way markings at a junction
colour: a double broken white line across your lane, often with a 'Give Way' triangle painted on the road
explanation: Double broken white lines across your half of the road mean give way to traffic on the major road ahead; slow down, be ready to stop, and only go when it is safe.
mnemonic: Two dashed lines: yield, don't stop sign.
notes: Composite road marking (TSRGD diagram 1003 family, often with 1023 triangle) drawn in-app; no single official SVG. Double broken transverse lines = give way (unlike a Stop line, which is a single solid transverse line).

caption: Zig-zag lines at a pedestrian crossing
colour: white zig-zag lines along both kerbs on the approach to and beyond a crossing
explanation: White zig-zag lines mark the controlled area at a pedestrian crossing where you must not park, overtake the lead vehicle, or wait; keep moving and give way to anyone on the crossing.
notes: Composite road marking (TSRGD diagram 1001.2 / zig-zag markings) drawn in-app; no single official SVG. Applies at zebra, pelican, puffin and toucan crossings (Highway Code rules 191-194, 240).

caption: Yellow box junction
colour: criss-cross yellow lines painted in a box across the junction
explanation: Yellow criss-cross lines mark a box junction you must not enter until your exit is clear, so you do not block the junction; you may wait in the box only when turning right and held up solely by oncoming traffic.
mnemonic: Keep the box clear: don't enter 'til you can leave.
notes: Composite road marking (TSRGD diagram 1043) drawn in-app; no single official SVG. Rider must not enter unless the exit is clear, except when turning right and stopped only by oncoming traffic (Highway Code rule 174).

caption: Centre line (ordinary)
colour: broken white line down the middle of the road, the painted dashes shorter than the gaps between them
explanation: A broken white line with short dashes and longer gaps marks the centre of the road. You may cross it to overtake or turn, but only when the road ahead is clear and it is safe.
mnemonic: Short dashes, long gaps: cross only if the way is clear.
searchTerms: dashed white line down the middle

caption: Lane line
colour: a short broken white line dividing a wide carriageway into lanes running the same direction, dashes short with longer gaps
explanation: Short broken white lines divide a wide road into lanes that run the same way. Keep to the centre of your lane and do not change lane unless it is clear and safe.
mnemonic: Lane line: stay in your lane.

caption: Edge of carriageway line
colour: a continuous solid white line running along the left-hand edge of the road, sometimes raised or ribbed
explanation: A continuous white line marks the edge of the carriageway and helps you judge your position, especially in poor visibility. Some versions are ribbed so you feel a rumble if your wheels stray onto them.
mnemonic: Solid line at the side: that's where the road ends.
searchTerms: white line at the side of the road

caption: Stop line
colour: a single solid white line painted across your lane at right angles to the kerb, at traffic signals or at a STOP sign
explanation: A solid white line across your lane marks where you must stop at traffic signals or at a STOP sign. Stop with your front wheel behind the line and do not cross it while the signal is red.
mnemonic: Solid line across: stop and hold behind it.
searchTerms: line across the road at lights
where to stop at the lights

caption: Lane direction arrows
colour: large white arrows painted along a lane (straight ahead, or curving left or right) telling you where that lane leads
explanation: White arrows painted on the road show which way each lane is meant to go. Get into the correct lane in good time and follow the direction the arrow indicates.
mnemonic: Follow the painted arrow to pick your lane.

caption: KEEP CLEAR marking
colour: the words KEEP CLEAR painted in large white letters on the carriageway, often outside a school entrance or access
explanation: A KEEP CLEAR marking tells you not to stop or queue across that part of the road, so the entrance or access stays clear. Do not let your motorcycle block it, even briefly.
mnemonic: KEEP CLEAR painted on the road: don't stop or block it.

caption: Bus lane marking
colour: the word BUS painted on the lane with a solid white line separating it from the rest of the road
explanation: A bus lane is marked by the word BUS on the road and a solid white line, with a sign showing its hours. Only use it within those hours if signs say you may; some bus lanes also allow motorcycles, but only where stated.
mnemonic: BUS on the road: not your lane unless a sign says so.

caption: Cycle lane marking
colour: a white cycle symbol painted on the lane, bordered by a solid or broken white line, sometimes on a coloured surface
explanation: A cycle lane is shown by a cycle symbol and a white line. Do not drive or park in a cycle lane bordered by a solid white line during its hours of operation; only enter one bordered by a broken line if it is unavoidable.
searchTerms: can I drive in a cycle lane

caption: Hatched and chevron markings
colour: an area of white diagonal stripes or chevrons painted on the road, bordered either by a solid white line or by a broken white line
explanation: Diagonal stripes or chevrons separate streams of traffic or protect vehicles turning right. If the border is a broken line, only enter when it is necessary and safe; if the border is a solid white line you must not enter except in an emergency.
mnemonic: Solid border: stay out. Broken border: only if safe.
searchTerms: white stripes in the middle of the road
can I drive over the chevrons

caption: SLOW marking
colour: the word SLOW painted in large white letters along the carriageway, usually approaching a hazard
explanation: A SLOW marking warns of a hazard ahead, such as a sharp bend or a junction. Ease off and reduce your speed before you reach it.
mnemonic: SLOW painted on the road: a hazard's close.

caption: Yellow waiting lines
colour: yellow lines running along the edge of the road parallel to the kerb: a single yellow line, or a double yellow line
explanation: A single yellow line means waiting is restricted during the times shown on nearby signs; a double yellow line means no waiting at any time, whether or not signs are present. You may still stop briefly to set down or pick up unless loading is also banned.
mnemonic: One line: check the times. Two lines: no waiting any time.
searchTerms: can I stop on yellow lines
yellow line at the side of the road

caption: Yellow kerb loading marks
colour: short yellow marks painted across (at right angles to) the kerb edge: a single mark, or a pair of marks
explanation: Yellow marks on the kerb show that loading is restricted: a single mark means loading is limited to the times on the nearby plate, and a pair of marks means no loading at any time. Check the plate before you stop to load.
mnemonic: Two kerb stripes: never load. One stripe: only at the times shown.
searchTerms: yellow lines on the pavement edge

caption: Red route lines
colour: red lines running along the edge of the road parallel to the kerb: a single red line, or a double red line (mainly in cities)
explanation: Red lines mark a Red Route, where stopping rules are stricter than yellow lines: a double red line means no stopping at any time, and a single red line means no stopping during the times shown on signs. You must not even stop to wait, except in a marked box.
mnemonic: Red means stopping's dead: don't stop at all.

caption: Reflective road studs (cat's eyes)
colour: reflective studs set into the road that glow in your headlights: red along the left edge, white between lanes, amber along the central reservation, and green at lay-bys and slip roads
explanation: Reflective road studs mark the road by colour: white marks the lanes or middle of the road, red marks the left edge, amber marks the central reservation, and green marks the carriageway edge at lay-bys and slip roads.
mnemonic: Red left, White middle, Amber central reservation; Green at slips.
